title: Natural Selection and Evolution
bigQuestion: How can a population change over generations, and what evidence shows that all living things share a family tree?

story.title: The Beak That Changed With the Rain
story.kicker: On a tiny island in the Galápagos, two scientists measured finches for decades and watched evolution happen.
paragraphs: In 1835 a young naturalist named Charles Darwin stepped off the ship HMS Beagle onto the Galápagos Islands, 1,000 kilometers off the coast of South America. He collected small brown birds. Only later, back in England, did an expert tell him they were all finches, a dozen or so species, each with a different beak. Some had thick beaks like nutcrackers. Some had thin ones like tweezers. Darwin wondered whether one kind of finch had reached the islands and, over ages, become many.

Nearly 140 years later, in 1973, Peter and Rosemary Grant landed on Daphne Major, a volcanic islet in the same archipelago with no people, no fresh water and one main species of ground finch. They decided to catch, band and measure every finch on the island, every year. Beak length, beak depth, wing, weight. Then they would follow each bird for life and record which ones had chicks.

In 1977 the rains did not come. Plants withered. The small soft seeds the finches liked were eaten first. What was left were big, tough seeds with hard cases. Finches died by the hundreds. The Grants found that the survivors were not a random sample. Birds with slightly deeper, stronger beaks could crack the tough seeds. Those birds lived. Thinner-beaked birds mostly starved.

The next spring, the survivors bred. Their chicks, on average, had deeper beaks than the chicks born before the drought. Beak depth is inherited, so the drought had shifted the whole population in one generation. A few years later, a very wet season flooded the island with small seeds, and the advantage flipped toward smaller beaks. The population shifted back.

The Grants kept measuring for more than forty years. Their notebooks hold the strongest direct record ever made of natural selection in the wild. Darwin had guessed the process was too slow to see. On a bare rock in the Pacific, it turned out to be fast enough to catch with a ruler, a scale and patience.
story.think: The drought did not change any single finch's beak. Yet the next generation's beaks were deeper on average. Explain how that is possible.

lessons.title: Layers of Time
lessons.mainIdea: Rock layers stack up over time, so deeper fossils are usually older, and the sequence shows how life on Earth has changed.
reading: Southwest of Chicago, near the town of Braidwood, old coal mine spoil piles hold round lumps of ironstone. Crack one open and you may find a fern leaf, a jellyfish, a shrimp, or the strange Tully monster, the state fossil of Illinois. These Mazon Creek fossils formed about 300 million years ago, when this land was a steamy swamp near the sea. A *fossil* is any preserved trace of a living thing from the past: a bone, a shell, a leaf print, a footprint.

Fossils form in layers of sediment. Mud settles on a river delta or sea floor, burying a dead animal. More mud settles on top. Over millions of years the layers harden into rock. In 1669 the Danish scientist Nicolas Steno stated the simple rule that follows: in undisturbed layers, the deepest layer formed first and the top formed last. This is the law of *superposition*. It lets geologists put fossils in order without any dates at all.

Read the layers from the bottom up and a story appears. The oldest rocks hold only fossils of microbes. Higher up appear soft sea animals, then shells, then fish, then the first land plants and insects, then amphibians, reptiles, dinosaurs, and only near the very top, mammals like us. The same order shows up on every continent. Fish never appear below the first microbes. Mammals never appear below the first fish.

Since the early 1900s, scientists have also measured the steady decay of radioactive elements in rock to attach real ages to layers. Those numbers agree with the order from superposition and give the timeline its scale: Earth is about 4.5 billion years old, and life has been here for most of that time.

words.d: a preserved trace of a living thing from the past, such as a bone, shell, print or footprint
the rule that in undisturbed rock layers, the deepest layer is the oldest and the top is the youngest
mud, sand and silt that settle in layers and can harden into rock

look.title: Milestones in the Rock Record
rows: Illinois coal swamps and Mazon Creek
look.cite: USGS and standard reference values, rounded
look.prompt: Microbes were alone on Earth for about 3 billion years before animals with shells appeared. What share of Earth's history is that, and what does it suggest about how slowly big changes happen?

check.q: In undisturbed rock layers, the fossils at the bottom are:
choices: The same age as the top
check.why: Layers pile up over time, so the deepest ones formed first. That is the law of superposition.

check.q: The Mazon Creek fossils of Illinois formed in what kind of environment?
check.why: About 300 million years ago, Illinois was a steamy swamp near the sea, which later became coal beds.

check.q: Which order of first appearance matches the fossil record?
check.why: The lowest layers hold only microbes, fish appear far above them, and mammals appear near the top.

lessons.title: Same Bones, Different Jobs
lessons.mainIdea: Animals as different as bats, whales and people share the same bone pattern in their limbs, evidence of a shared ancestor.
reading: Lay out the front limb of a human, a cat, a bat and a whale side by side. The jobs could not be more different: grasping, running, flying, swimming. Yet the bones match. One upper bone. Two lower bones. A cluster of wrist bones. Then five sets of finger bones, stretched long and thin in the bat's wing, shortened and buried inside the whale's flipper. Structures that share a common pattern because they came from a shared ancestor are called *homologous*.

If an engineer designed a wing from scratch, it would not need five finger bones. A flipper would not need a wrist. The most reasonable explanation is that all four animals inherited the pattern from a common ancestor that lived long ago, and each line changed it for a different use. This is the same reasoning you would use if four cousins all had the same unusual nose.

Not every likeness means kinship. A bird's wing and an insect's wing both fly, but inside they are built completely differently. Bird wings are modified arms. Insect wings are outgrowths of the body wall with no bones. Structures that do the same job but are built differently are called *analogous*. They show that different lines can arrive at similar solutions. Homologous parts show shared ancestry; analogous parts do not.

words.d: structures in different species that share a pattern because they came from a common ancestor
structures that do a similar job but are built differently and did not come from a shared pattern
a species from which two or more later species descended

look.title: Four Limbs on the Table
look.text: A museum drawer holds X-rays of four front limbs. Limb 1 is short with a thick upper bone and five spread fingers. Limb 2 has extremely long, thin finger bones with skin between them. Limb 3 is a flat paddle with all five fingers packed inside. Limb 4 has a single upper bone, two lower bones and hooves at the end, with the finger bones merged into one.
look.prompt: Which animals might these be? What single pattern do all four share, and why is that pattern strong evidence for a shared ancestor?

check.q: A bat wing and a human arm have the same bones in the same order. These structures are:
check.why: Same pattern, different job, inherited from a shared ancestor: that is homology.

check.q: A bird's wing and a butterfly's wing both fly but are built completely differently. They are:
choices: Proof of a recent common ancestor
check.why: Analogous structures do a similar job but arose separately, from different starting parts.

check.q: Why do whales have finger bones inside their flippers?
choices: They use them to grab fish
They inherited the pattern from land-living ancestors
All swimming animals have finger bones
The bones grow in from the water
check.why: The buried finger bones do little for swimming. They are leftovers from a four-limbed ancestor.

lessons.title: Embryos and Leftover Parts
lessons.mainIdea: Early embryos of different animals look alike, and many animals carry useless leftover parts, both signs of shared descent.
reading: A few weeks after fertilization, an embryo of a fish, a chicken and a human look surprisingly alike. Each has a tail. Each has a row of small pouches along the neck. In the fish, those pouches become gills. In the chicken and the human, they become parts of the jaw, ear and throat. Similar early stages that later diverge are what you would expect if the animals share an ancestor and each line modified the same starting plan.

Adults carry clues too. Whales have small hip bones floating in their flesh, attached to nothing. Some snakes have tiny leg bones under their skin. Humans have a tailbone made of fused bones, muscles for wiggling our ears that most of us cannot use, and an appendix that we can live without. Parts like these, reduced and with little or no use, are called *vestigial* structures.

A vestigial part is hard to explain if each species was built fresh for its way of life. It is easy to explain if the part was useful in an ancestor and shrank in later generations once it stopped mattering. The whale's hip bones make sense because the whale's ancestors walked on land, and fossils of early whales with legs, found in Pakistan and Egypt, back that up.

words.d: an animal in its earliest stage of development, before birth or hatching
a body part that is reduced and has little or no use, left over from an ancestor
to become different over time after starting out alike

look.title: The Whale's Hip
look.text: A museum skeleton of a blue whale is 25 meters long. Near the tail end, hanging below the spine and attached to no other bone, are two small curved bones about the size of a person's hand. A label says they are hip bones. In a fossil whale from about 45 million years ago, the same bones are large and attached to short hind legs.
look.prompt: Why would a modern whale carry hip bones it does not use? How does the fossil support your answer?

check.q: Which is an example of a vestigial structure?
check.why: The whale's hip bones have no working legs attached and are leftovers from land-living ancestors.

check.q: Early embryos of fish, chickens and humans all have neck pouches. What does this suggest?
choices: All three breathe with gills as adults
Humans are a kind of fish
They share an ancestor and modified the same early plan
Embryos are all identical until birth
check.why: Shared early stages that later diverge fit descent from a common ancestor.

check.q: Fossil whales with legs were found in Pakistan and Egypt. This evidence:
choices: Shows whales never lived in the sea
Supports the idea that whales descended from land animals
Has nothing to do with modern whales
check.why: Legged fossil whales connect land-living ancestors to modern whales with vestigial hips.

lessons.title: Variation Is Everywhere
lessons.mainIdea: Individuals in every population differ, and many of those differences are inherited, which gives natural selection something to act on.
reading: Line up twenty acorns from one oak. No two are the same size. Measure twenty ground finches, as the Grants did, and beak depth ranges over several millimeters. Look around your classroom. Heights, hair, the shape of an earlobe, how well someone tastes bitter foods. *Variation* is the rule in every population, not the exception. Much of it comes from mutation and from the shuffling of alleles in sexual reproduction.

Not all variation counts for evolution. A finch that lost a toe in an accident will not pass that on. Only *heritable* variation, differences carried in genes, can move from parents to offspring. The Grants tested this on Daphne Major. Parents with deep beaks had chicks with deep beaks, on average, even in years with plenty of food. Beak depth was heritable.

Darwin's first insight was simply to take variation seriously. Before him, many naturalists treated the differences among individuals as noise around an ideal type. Darwin saw that the differences were the raw material. If some variants survive and reproduce more than others, and the variants are inherited, the population must change. Everything else follows from that.

words.d: differences among individuals in a population
able to be passed from parents to offspring through genes
the starting stuff that a process works on; for evolution, heritable variation

look.title: Beaks on a Chart
look.text: The Grants measured beak depth in 750 ground finches on Daphne Major in a normal year. Plotted on a chart, the beaks ranged from about 8 millimeters to about 11 millimeters, with most near the middle and a few at each end. Chicks of deep-beaked parents fell mostly on the deep side; chicks of shallow-beaked parents fell mostly on the shallow side.
look.prompt: What two facts about this population does the chart establish? Why does natural selection need both?

check.q: Which of these variations can natural selection act on?
choices: A tan from the summer sun
check.why: Only heritable differences, carried in genes, can be passed on and shift a population.

check.q: Where does most heritable variation come from?
choices: Mutation and the shuffling of alleles in sexual reproduction
check.why: New alleles arise by mutation, and sexual reproduction mixes them into new combinations.

check.q: The Grants found that deep-beaked parents had deep-beaked chicks. This showed that beak depth is:
check.why: The trait passed from parents to offspring, which means genes control much of it.

lessons.title: More Are Born Than Survive
lessons.mainIdea: Every species produces more offspring than the environment can support, so most die before reproducing, and which ones survive is not random.
reading: A single oak can drop thousands of acorns in a year. A cod lays millions of eggs. A pair of finches can raise several clutches. If every offspring lived, the world would be buried in oaks, cod and finches within a few centuries. It is not. Populations stay roughly steady over long stretches, which means most offspring die before they reproduce. Darwin called this the struggle for existence.

Darwin got the idea partly from an economist. In 1798 Thomas Malthus wrote that human populations tend to grow faster than their food supply, so hunger, disease and conflict hold them back. Darwin read Malthus in 1838 and saw the same logic in every species. The pressure never lets up. Food, water, space, predators and disease keep numbers in check, just as the limiting factors in the ecosystems chapter do.

Here is the key step. If survival were pure luck, the survivors would be a random sample and nothing would change. But survival is not pure luck. In the 1977 drought, finches with deeper beaks survived far more often than thin-beaked ones. Individuals whose heritable traits fit the environment better survive and reproduce more. Darwin named this *natural selection*: nature, not a breeder, does the choosing.

words.d: the process in which individuals with traits that fit their environment survive and reproduce more, so those traits become more common
Darwin's name for the fact that more offspring are born than can survive
when a species makes far more offspring than the environment can support

look.title: Malthus on Population and Food
look.text: Population, when unchecked, increases in a geometrical ratio. Subsistence increases only in an arithmetical ratio.
look.cite: Thomas Malthus, An Essay on the Principle of Population, 1798
look.prompt: A geometrical ratio doubles: 2, 4, 8, 16. An arithmetical one adds: 2, 4, 6, 8. Why did this idea about people help Darwin explain finches and oaks?

check.q: A cod lays millions of eggs, but cod populations do not explode. Why?
choices: Most eggs and young die before reproducing
Cod stop laying eggs when crowded
Each cod lives only one year
check.why: Overproduction plus limited resources means most offspring never survive to reproduce.

check.q: What did Darwin take from Malthus?
choices: The idea that species never change
The idea that populations outgrow their resources, causing a struggle for existence
check.why: Malthus argued populations grow faster than food. Darwin applied that pressure to every species.

check.q: For natural selection to change a population, which must be true?
choices: Individuals with certain heritable traits must survive and reproduce more than others
check.why: Selection requires that survival depend, at least partly, on inherited traits.

lessons.title: Selection Step by Step
lessons.mainIdea: Natural selection changes a population over generations by making helpful heritable traits more common, and the result is adaptation.
reading: Put the pieces together and follow one generation on Daphne Major. Step one: variation. Finch beaks range from shallow to deep, and the difference is inherited. Step two: overproduction. More chicks hatch than the island can feed. Step three: selection. A drought leaves only tough seeds, and deep-beaked birds crack them and survive while others starve. Step four: inheritance. The survivors breed, and their chicks inherit deeper beaks.

The result is a shift in the whole population. The average beak got deeper. No finch changed its own beak, and no finch tried to grow a deeper one. The population changed because some finches left more descendants than others. Repeat those four steps for thousands of generations and small shifts add up to big ones. A trait that spreads because it helps survival and reproduction in a particular environment is an *adaptation*.

Two warnings. First, selection has no goal. When wet years brought small seeds, smaller beaks did better and the population shifted back. The environment decides what is helpful, and the environment changes. Second, selection can only work with variation that already exists. If no finch had carried genes for a deeper beak, the drought would have simply killed finches. Mutation supplies new options; selection sorts them.

This is also how new species arise. Split a population, say on two islands with different seeds. Let selection push each in a different direction for long enough, and the two groups may become so different that they no longer interbreed. Darwin's dozen finch species, with their dozen beaks, are what that process looks like after a few million years.

words.d: a heritable trait that has become common because it helps survival and reproduction in a particular environment
one round of parents and their offspring
a group of organisms that can breed with one another and produce fertile offspring

look.title: Darwin Sees a Pattern
look.text: Seeing this gradation and diversity of structure in one small, intimately related group of birds, one might really fancy that from an original paucity of birds in this archipelago, one species had been taken and modified for different ends.
look.cite: Charles Darwin, Journal of Researches (The Voyage of the Beagle), 1845
look.prompt: Darwin says one species may have been modified for different ends. Using the four steps of natural selection, explain how one finch could become many.

check.q: Which is the correct order of steps in natural selection?
check.why: Varied individuals are born in excess, some survive better because of their traits, and they pass those traits on.

check.q: During the drought, what actually changed?
choices: Each finch grew a deeper beak
Finches decided to eat harder seeds
The share of finches with deep beaks in the population
The finches' genes changed on purpose
check.why: Individuals do not change. The population shifts because deep-beaked birds left more offspring.

check.q: Why did the population shift back toward smaller beaks in wet years?
choices: Finches got tired of big seeds
Small seeds were plentiful, so small-beaked birds did better
check.why: Selection has no fixed direction. When the environment changed, a different trait became helpful.

lessons.title: Germs That Fight Back
lessons.mainIdea: Bacteria evolve resistance to antibiotics by natural selection, fast enough to see in hospitals within years.
reading: In 1928 Alexander Fleming noticed that a mold growing on one of his dishes had killed the bacteria around it. The mold made penicillin, the first *antibiotic*, a drug that kills bacteria or stops them from growing. By the mid-1940s penicillin was saving soldiers' lives. Within a few years, doctors were already finding bacteria it no longer killed.

The reason is natural selection running at high speed. Bacteria divide every twenty minutes or so, and a single infection holds billions of cells. Among those billions, a few carry a mutation that lets them survive the drug: an enzyme that chops it up, or a pump that pushes it out. Give the antibiotic, and the drug kills the sensitive cells. The rare *resistant* cells survive, divide, and soon make up the whole population.

Two habits make the problem worse. Stopping a prescription early leaves the toughest survivors behind. Using antibiotics when they are not needed, such as for a viral cold, gives bacteria more chances to be selected. Today the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention counts millions of resistant infections and tens of thousands of deaths in the United States each year, and some strains resist nearly every drug we have.

The fight is a race. Scientists search soil and sea for new antibiotics, and doctors work to use existing ones carefully. Every step follows the same rules the finches did: variation, overproduction, selection, inheritance. Here, though, a generation lasts minutes, not years.

words.d: a medicine that kills bacteria or stops them from growing
able to survive something that would normally kill or harm, such as a bacterium that survives an antibiotic
a group of bacteria of one species that share a particular set of traits

look.title: Fleming's Warning
look.text: In his Nobel lecture in 1945, Fleming warned that penicillin was easy to buy and easy to underdose. He described how a person who took too little could expose microbes to an amount of the drug that did not kill them, and could thereby make them resistant, and he imagined that resistant microbes could then be passed to other people.
look.prompt: Fleming was describing natural selection without using the phrase. Which of the four steps does underdosing affect most?

check.q: How do bacteria become resistant to an antibiotic?
choices: Each bacterium learns to tolerate the drug
Rare cells with a resistance mutation survive and multiply while sensitive cells die
The drug changes the bacteria's DNA on purpose
Bacteria share the drug among themselves
check.why: The drug selects for the few already-resistant cells. Their descendants take over the population.

check.q: Why does bacterial resistance evolve so much faster than finch beaks?
choices: Bacteria reproduce every few minutes and exist in the billions
check.why: Short generations and huge numbers give selection many more rounds and more mutations to work with.

check.q: Taking antibiotics for a viral cold:
choices: Does not help the cold and gives bacteria more chances to be selected for resistance
check.why: Antibiotics do not act on viruses, and needless use selects for resistant bacteria in the body.

lessons.title: Breeding as a Model
lessons.mainIdea: Darwin used the breeding of pigeons, dogs and crops as a model for natural selection: the same process, with a breeder instead of the environment choosing.
reading: Darwin kept pigeons. He joined pigeon clubs in London and studied fancy breeds with fan tails, feathered feet, puffed chests and tumbling flight. All of them, breeders agreed, came from one wild species, the rock pigeon. If human choice could turn one bird into dozens of forms in a few centuries, Darwin reasoned, what could nature's choice do in millions of years? He opened the Origin of Species with pigeons for exactly that reason.

Breeding by people is called *artificial selection*. The steps mirror natural selection: variation exists, a breeder chooses which individuals reproduce, and the offspring inherit the chosen traits. The difference is who chooses and why. A breeder picks the sweetest corn or the fastest horse. The environment picks whatever survives and breeds, with no plan at all.

You can run the model yourself. On the site's turntables, spin a disk of colored beans and pick out only the darkest ten each round, then imagine those breed and the next round has more dark beans. Or track a real case: the University of Illinois corn experiment has chosen high-oil kernels every year since 1896, and oil content has climbed far beyond anything in the starting field. Selection, repeated, moves a population a long way.

words.d: breeding in which people choose which individuals reproduce based on the traits they want
the wild pigeon species from which all fancy pigeon breeds were bred

look.title: Wolf to Whippet
look.text: Every dog, from a 2-kilogram Chihuahua to a 70-kilogram mastiff, descends from gray wolves that people began keeping at least 15,000 years ago. A wolf and a whippet look nothing alike, yet they can still interbreed, and DNA shows they are the same species. Nearly every breed we know today was shaped by breeders in just the last few hundred years.
look.prompt: What does the dog story show about how much selection can change a population in a short time? What could it not have done without variation among wolves?

check.q: In artificial selection, who or what decides which individuals reproduce?
check.why: Breeders choose parents with the traits they want. In natural selection the environment does the sorting.

check.q: Why did Darwin begin the Origin of Species with pigeons?
choices: Breeding showed how much selection can change a species in a short time
Pigeons are unrelated to other birds
check.why: Human selection of pigeons was a model readers could see for what natural selection could do over ages.

check.q: Artificial and natural selection are alike because both:
choices: Work on existing heritable variation and change a population over generations
check.why: Both need variation and inheritance. They differ only in who does the choosing.

lessons.title: How the Idea Grew
lessons.mainIdea: Darwin and Wallace proposed natural selection in 1858, and later discoveries in genetics and DNA filled in what they could not know.
reading: Darwin returned from the Beagle in 1836 and worked on his idea for twenty years, filling notebooks and breeding pigeons. In 1858 a letter arrived from Alfred Russel Wallace, a naturalist collecting in the islands of Southeast Asia. Wallace had reached the same idea on his own. Friends arranged for both men's papers to be read together at a scientific meeting in London that year. Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859.

Darwin had a serious gap. He did not know how traits were inherited. Mendel's pea paper appeared in 1866, but Darwin never saw it, and no one connected the two until after 1900. In the twentieth century, genes, chromosomes and mutations gave natural selection its missing piece: a way for variation to arise and be passed on. Then in 1953 the structure of DNA was worked out, and the code itself came into view.

DNA turned out to be the strongest evidence of all. Every living thing uses the same code of four bases and the same basic set of amino acids. Species that fossils and anatomy suggested were close relatives also turned out to have the most similar DNA. Scientists can now draw the family tree of life from DNA alone, and it matches the tree drawn from bones and rocks.

Evolution is not a claim that living things are getting better, or that any change is planned. It is the observation that populations change over generations, plus the explanation, tested for more than 160 years, of how that happens. Like every good scientific idea, it is still being refined, but its core has survived every test so far.

words.d: in science, a well-tested explanation supported by a large body of evidence
one of the small units that link together to form a protein
observations and measurements that support or challenge an idea

look.title: Darwin's Last Sentence
look.text: There is grandeur in this view of life, with its several powers, having been originally breathed into a few forms or into one; and that, whilst this planet has gone cycling on according to the fixed law of gravity, from so simple a beginning endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful have been, and are being, evolved.
look.cite: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species, 1859
look.prompt: Darwin writes that forms are being evolved, in the present tense. What evidence from this chapter shows evolution still going on today?

check.q: Who reached the idea of natural selection independently of Darwin?
check.why: Wallace's 1858 letter from Southeast Asia described the same idea, and both papers were read together in London.

check.q: What important piece was missing from Darwin's explanation in 1859?
check.why: Darwin did not know about genes. Mendel's work and later DNA research filled that gap.

check.q: Which finding from DNA supports the family tree of life?
choices: Every species has its own separate genetic code
Species that look related by bones also have the most similar DNA
DNA is found only in animals
check.why: Independent evidence from DNA matches the tree built from anatomy and fossils.

lessons.title: Cousins, Not Parents
lessons.mainIdea: Humans did not descend from chimpanzees; humans and the great apes share common ancestors, with chimpanzees as our closest living relatives.
reading: Stand a human skeleton beside a chimpanzee skeleton. The bones match one for one: same skull plan, same 206 or so bones, same five fingers with a thumb. Humans and chimpanzees share about 98 to 99 percent of their DNA sequence. Gorillas are a little more distant, orangutans a little more still. Together with humans, these animals are the great apes.

A common mistake is to say humans came from chimps. They did not. Chimpanzees are cousins, not ancestors. Both lines descend from a common ancestor that lived in Africa roughly six or seven million years ago. That ancestor was neither a modern chimp nor a modern human. One line led to today's chimpanzees and bonobos. Another line, with many branches, led to us. Every other branch on our side has died out.

Chromosomes give a striking clue. Chimpanzees, gorillas and orangutans have 48 chromosomes; humans have 46. Human chromosome 2 carries, end to end, the same genes found on two separate ape chromosomes, with leftover pieces at the join. Two ancestral chromosomes fused into one somewhere along the human line. That is exactly what a shared ancestry predicts and very hard to explain any other way.

words.d: the group that includes orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees, bonobos and humans
to come from an earlier ancestor through many generations
joined into one; two ancestral chromosomes fused to form human chromosome 2

look.title: The Family Photo
look.text: Imagine a family reunion. You and your second cousin are the same age. You did not come from your cousin, and your cousin did not come from you. You both came from the same great-grandparents, who are no longer living. Now replace yourself with all humans, your cousin with all chimpanzees, and the great-grandparents with an ape population that lived in Africa millions of years ago.
look.prompt: Why is "humans came from chimpanzees" the wrong way to say it? What is the right way?

check.q: Which statement is correct?
choices: Humans and chimpanzees share a common ancestor
check.why: Both lines descend from an ape ancestor that lived millions of years ago and was neither species.

check.q: Humans have 46 chromosomes and chimpanzees have 48. What explains this?
choices: Humans lost two whole chromosomes of genes
Two ancestral chromosomes fused into one in the human line
Chimpanzees gained two new chromosomes with no genes
check.why: Human chromosome 2 matches two ape chromosomes joined end to end.

check.q: Which is our closest living relative?
check.why: DNA and anatomy both place chimpanzees and bonobos closest to humans among living species.

lessons.title: Fossils of Early Humans
lessons.mainIdea: Fossils from Africa show a branching human family over millions of years, with upright walking coming long before large brains.
reading: In 1974, in the Afar region of Ethiopia, scientists found about 40 percent of a small skeleton in rock about 3.2 million years old. They nicknamed her Lucy. Her hips, knees and spine show she walked upright on two legs, yet her brain was about the size of a chimpanzee's and her arms were long for climbing. Lucy belongs to a species called Australopithecus afarensis, one of many extinct relatives on the human branch.

Lucy overturned an old guess. Many scientists had expected big brains to come first and upright walking later. The fossils say the opposite. Upright walking appears by around four million years ago. Brains stayed small for a long time afterward and grew mainly in the last two million years, along with stone tools, control of fire, and eventually language and art.

The family tree is bushy, not a ladder. At several times, more than one kind of human relative lived at once. Neanderthals lived in Europe and Asia until about 40,000 years ago and even interbred with our ancestors; many people today carry a small amount of Neanderthal DNA. Our own species, Homo sapiens, appears in Africa about 300,000 years ago and then spread across the world. Every person alive today belongs to that one species.

words.d: the scientific name for modern humans, the only living species on the human branch
an extinct human relative that lived in Europe and Asia until about 40,000 years ago
moving on two legs with the body held vertical, a key early human trait

look.title: Reading Lucy's Bones
look.text: Lucy's knee joint angles inward so that her feet sat under her body's center, the way a human's do and unlike a chimp's bowed legs. Her pelvis is short and wide like a human's. Her skull, though, held a brain of roughly 400 cubic centimeters, close to a chimpanzee's, and her arms were long compared with her legs.
look.prompt: Which of Lucy's traits are human-like and which are ape-like? What does the mix tell you about the order in which human traits appeared?

check.q: What did Lucy's skeleton show came first in human evolution?
check.why: Lucy walked upright 3.2 million years ago but had a small, ape-sized brain.

check.q: The human family tree is best described as:
choices: A single ladder from ape to human
A bush with many branches, most now extinct
A straight line with no branches
check.why: Several human relatives lived at the same time in the past. Only Homo sapiens survives.

check.q: Where and roughly when did Homo sapiens first appear?
check.why: The earliest fossils of our own species come from Africa around 300,000 years ago. Lucy, at 3.2 million years, was a different species.

review.q: In a cliff of undisturbed rock layers, where would you expect the oldest fossils?
choices: Anywhere, since layers do not show age
review.why: Superposition: the deepest layers were laid down first.

review.q: A human arm, a cat leg, a bat wing and a whale flipper share the same bone pattern. This is evidence of:
review.why: Homologous structures with the same pattern point to inheritance from a shared ancestor.

review.q: During the 1977 drought on Daphne Major, which finches were most likely to survive?
review.why: Only large, tough seeds remained, and deeper beaks could crack them.

review.q: Which is NOT one of the four requirements for natural selection?
review.why: Individuals do not change themselves. Populations change because some individuals leave more descendants.

choices: Rare resistant mutants survive the drug and multiply
review.why: The drug kills sensitive cells and leaves resistant ones to take over, which is natural selection.

review.q: How does artificial selection differ from natural selection?
choices: A person chooses which individuals reproduce
review.why: Both work on heritable variation, but in artificial selection a breeder does the choosing.

choices: Any change an animal makes during its life
A heritable trait that became common because it aids survival and reproduction
review.why: Adaptations are inherited traits shaped by natural selection, not changes within one lifetime.

review.q: The relationship between humans and chimpanzees is best described as:
choices: Both descended from a common ancestor millions of years ago
review.why: Chimpanzees are our closest living cousins, not our ancestors.
